facts: The request body `token` is attacker-controlled (@RequestBody) — observed at PreferencesController.java:16.
The decoded bytes are passed to ObjectInputStream.readObject() with no ObjectInputFilter and no resolveClass() override — observed at PreferencesController.java:18-19.
conclusions: Arbitrary classes on the classpath are instantiated during readObject(), before any type is checked.
Whether this reaches remote code execution depends on a usable gadget chain among the service's transitive dependencies.
hypotheses: A Spring-core style gadget is plausibly reachable on a Spring Boot classpath, but this has NOT been confirmed against this project's dependency tree.

threat.actor: Unauthenticated remote caller who can POST to the endpoint.
preconditions: A usable gadget chain on the classpath (for RCE); none needed for DoS
threat.attacker_input: A base64-encoded, crafted Java serialized object graph in the request body.
threat.violated_property: Integrity of code execution (untrusted data must not become executable object graphs).
threat.availability_impact: High (deserialization bombs cause CPU/memory exhaustion without any gadget)
threat.attack_narrative: Attacker crafts a serialized payload -> posts it -> ObjectInputStream reconstructs the attacker's object graph -> gadget chain executes during readObject().

security_objective: Untrusted, client-supplied bytes must never drive native Java object reconstruction.

candidates.approach: Stop using native Java serialization on the wire. Accept the preferences as a JSON DTO bound by Jackson with default typing disabled, and delete the ObjectInputStream path.
candidates.security_mechanism: Format change to a non-executable data format with no polymorphic type resolution.
advantages: Eliminates the root cause: no readObject() sink remains.
limitations: Breaks wire compatibility with clients that send the serialized token.
bypass_risks: Only if Jackson polymorphic/default typing is later enabled.
validation_requirements: A JSON body binds and applies.
A native serialized payload is rejected as malformed input.

candidates.approach: Keep ObjectInputStream but install a strict allow-list ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290) with maxdepth/maxrefs budgets.
limitations: The allow-list must be maintained; an over-broad pattern re-opens the hole.
bypass_risks: A too-permissive filter pattern can still admit a gadget.
behavioral_risks: Legitimate but unlisted nested types would be rejected.
validation_requirements: A non-allow-listed class is rejected before instantiation.

evaluation.new_weakness: none if default typing stays off
evaluation.simpler_safer_alt: this is the simplest safe option

recommendation.why_selected: It removes the root cause entirely and is the smallest change that fully restores the security objective.
recommendation.why_alternatives_rejected: CAND-002 only constrains the sink and depends on an allow-list that silently re-opens the hole if mis-maintained.
recommendation.security_property_restored: Untrusted input can no longer cause instantiation of arbitrary classes.
recommendation.expected_behavior_after: Preferences are submitted as JSON; serialized tokens are rejected as malformed input.
known_limitations: Existing clients sending the serialized token must migrate to JSON.
recommendation.residual_risk: Low, provided Jackson default typing is never enabled on this path. Novel, internally-derived recommendation: human review required.

validation_requirements.assertion: A valid JSON preferences body is applied.
A native Java serialized payload is no longer deserialized.
No ObjectInputStream.readObject() on request-derived bytes remains (SAST/grep gate).

provenance.reasoning: Internally derived from the vulnerability evidence and established secure-coding principles for CWE-502. No external citation is claimed; confidence is Low.
